title: Family & Relationships
summary: Short ideas on marriage, fatherhood and being listened to.

cards.hook: Couples who split don't fight more. They fight with contempt.
cards.body: John Gottman spent decades watching couples argue. He named four patterns that predict trouble: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Contempt, which includes sarcasm, eye-rolling and mockery, is the most corrosive of the four, because it says 'I'm better than you'. Disagreement is normal. Disrespect is the thing to catch in yourself.
cards.deeper: Each horseman has an antidote. Replace criticism with a complaint about one specific thing. Replace contempt by building a culture of appreciation. Replace defensiveness by taking even partial responsibility. And when you're flooded and about to stonewall, say you need a break, then come back.

source.ref: Gottman & Silver, *The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work*, Ch. 2

cards.hook: How an argument starts mostly decides how it ends.
cards.body: Gottman found that a conversation which opens harshly almost always ends badly. A softened start-up means describing the problem and your feelings without blame, and asking for what you need. 'You never help' invites a fight. 'I'm worn out tonight and I'd love a hand with the dishes' invites a conversation.

source.ref: Gottman & Silver, *The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work*, Principle 5: Solve Your Solvable Problems

cards.hook: Ask her something about her inner world you couldn't answer yesterday.
cards.body: Gottman's first principle is to build 'love maps': a detailed picture of your partner's world, including worries, hopes, friends and small preferences. Couples who know each other's world handle stress better. Tonight, ask one real question: what's weighing on her this month, or what she's looking forward to. Then just listen.

source.ref: Gottman & Silver, *The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work*, Principle 1: Enhance Your Love Maps

cards.hook: Telling an upset child 'you're fine' makes things louder, not quieter.
cards.body: Faber and Mazlish argue that denying a child's feelings ('it's nothing', 'you don't mean that') teaches them to stop trusting their own experience. Naming the feeling works better: 'You're really disappointed. You were looking forward to it.' It feels odd at first and then it works, because the child feels understood and can move on to solving the problem.

source.ref: Faber & Mazlish, *How to Talk So Kids Will Listen & Listen So Kids Will Talk*, Ch. 1

cards.hook: When your child melts down, try to name it before you fix it.
cards.body: Siegel and Bryson call it 'name it to tame it'. Putting words to a big feeling helps a child's thinking brain catch up with the emotional one. Today, the next time your child is upset, skip the lecture and say what you see: 'You're furious that we have to leave.' Then wait. Notice how quickly the temperature drops.

source.ref: Siegel & Bryson, *The Whole-Brain Child*, strategy 'Name It to Tame It'
